turns.boundedConclusion: BC 1014.2 sets a uniform ordinary handrail range of 34–38 inches, measured above stair-tread nosings or the finished ramp slope. Alternating tread devices and ships ladders have a separate uniform 30–34-inch range measured above tread nosings. The section permits specified fittings or bendings to exceed the maximum, and permits a guard’s top surface to be used as a handrail along stepped or ramped aisles where BC 1029.15 permits. The supplied text does not include BC 1014.3, needed to establish the referenced graspability requirements relevant to the guard alternative.

Fittings or bendings used to provide a continuous transition between flights may exceed the maximum height.

In Group R-3 occupancies; within dwelling units in Group R-2; and in Group U occupancies associated with Group R-3 or with individual Group R-2 dwelling units, fittings or bendings may exceed the maximum at the fittings or bendings when used for a continuous transition between flights, a transition at winder treads, a transition from handrail to guard, or at the start of a flight.

The top surface of a guard may be used as a handrail along stepped and ramped aisles only where permitted in accordance with BC 1029.15. That section covers stepped aisles and ramped aisles exceeding a 1:15 slope; it includes an alternative involving a side guard whose top surface meets the referenced handrail graspability requirements.

turns.boundedConclusion: BC 1014.6 requires handrails to return to a wall, guard, or walking surface, or to continue to the handrail of an adjacent stair flight or ramp run. For noncontinuous stair handrails, it requires a horizontal extension of at least 12 inches beyond the top riser and a sloped continuation for one tread depth beyond the bottom riser. Noncontinuous ramp handrails must extend horizontally above the landing at least 12 inches beyond both the top and bottom of the ramp runs. The section also states direction requirements and four exceptions; assembly-aisle handrails may use the extension provisions of BC 1029.15, which dispenses with extensions at aisle tops and bottoms to permit crossovers. The stated exceptions remain conditional on their specified dwelling-unit, aisle, or stair-device contexts.

materialChecks.criterion: Handrails must return to a wall, guard, or walking surface, or be continuous to the handrail of an adjacent flight of stairs or ramp run.

Where stair handrails are not continuous between flights, they must extend horizontally at least 12 inches beyond the top riser and continue to slope for one tread depth beyond the bottom riser. Stair extensions must be in the direction of the stair flights.

Where ramp handrails are not continuous between runs, they must extend horizontally above the landing at least 12 inches beyond both the top and bottom of the ramp runs. Ramp extensions must be in the direction of the ramp runs.
A handrail within a dwelling unit that is not an Accessible unit, Type B+NYC unit, or Type B unit need extend only from the top riser to the bottom riser.
A handrail within a Type B+NYC multistory dwelling unit that complies with BC 1107.2.5, Items 1 through 3, need extend only from the top riser to the bottom riser.

Handrails serving aisles in rooms or spaces used for assembly purposes are permitted to follow BC 1029.15 for extensions. Under BC 1029.15, extensions are not required at the top and bottom of stepped or ramped aisles to permit crossovers within the aisles.

Handrails for alternating tread devices and ships ladders may terminate vertically above the top and bottom risers; they need not be continuous between flights or extend beyond the top or bottom risers.
